dek: A pick shop founded in 1971 by Morris "Doc" Moseman, now selling a roster of more than a dozen handicappers and computer systems. Packages ran from $25 a day to $850 a season on 20 Nov 2026. Its guarantee pays in more picks or store credit, never cash, and every record on its site is a run or total the seller chose.

short_answer: Doc's Sports is a real, long running business. A 2012 Gambling911 obituary says Morris "Doc" Moseman started it in 1971 and ran it for more than 40 years, with his son helping move it onto the web. Today the site names an operator, Doc's Enterprises, a Wisconsin mailing address, a toll free phone line with posted hours, and a full price list. In that narrow sense it is legitimate.

Whether its picks make money is a different question, and nothing we could open answers it. The site shows streaks such as "193-134 +12,705" or "+17,430 Soccer Run!" chosen by the seller, with no full log of every pick, price and post time. We checked the numbers it does post: the win rates match their own win and loss counts, but the same record is often given two different ways on one page, and the founding story gives four different ages for the business.

Independent buyer posts we found run mostly negative, from Covers in 2008 to TheRX in 2026, with a few positive voices on SBR and one five star PissedConsumer review. The guarantee gives losing buyers more picks or a store credit, not their money back. Treat Doc's Sports as a seller with marketing records, not a proven winner. If you buy, buy short, log every pick yourself with the line and time you received it, and judge it after a few hundred picks.

guarantee: The guarantee is the core of the pitch ("You Win or We Work for Free!"), so read the wording package by package. On weekly and monthly packages the page says that if the package "finishes at a loss, you can extend your service for free through our self-extend program." On one day packages the remedy is an account credit, usually $25 or $30, added around 11 a.m. Eastern the next morning. The NBA day credit reads: "If your package finishes at a loss, a $30 credit will be added to your account the following morning".

Several day packages count a small profit as a failure too. The college basketball day package says that "If the package does not produce at least $40 in profit across all plays, a $30 account credit will be applied", and the NHL day package pays the credit on "a loss (or profit less than $35)". The four season and year long packages ($495 football, $849 college basketball, $850 NBA, $795 NHL and soccer) carry no guarantee wording at all on the page we read.

We found no cash refund terms on any Doc's Sports page we opened, and the terms of service link we tried returned a not found error. A buyer who loses money betting the picks gets more picks from the same handicapper or credit to spend at the same store. Losses on the bets themselves are never covered, and those are usually far larger than the package price. A Covers forum member wrote in 2016 that the service only offers more picks until you recover your losses, which matches the written terms.

claims_note: How we checked. We took every record on the homepage, the roster page, the house handicapper page and the college basketball special that gives both wins and losses, divided wins by wins plus losses, and compared the result with the percentage the seller printed. Every printed percentage we tested matched its own counts after rounding: for example 599 of 997 is 60.1% and 117 of 201 is 58.2%. So the arithmetic inside each blurb is honest. What the blurbs leave out is the start date, the prices taken, the unit sizes and every losing run around each streak.

We then compared the same record where it appears twice. On the house handicapper page alone, the football season profit is +3,010 in the sidebar and +3,090 in the member notes, the soccer run is +17,430 in one place and +17,830 in another, the UFC run is 16-6 for +4,715 in one place and 16-5 for +5,135 in another, and the NHL profit of +9,840 is labelled 2025 in the sidebar and 2026 in the text. The homepage soccer line says 25-7 on 7 unit plays while the roster says 27-7. These may be updates that did not reach every box, but a buyer cannot tell which number is current.

The dollar figures are explained nowhere we looked. They usually mean profit for a bettor risking $100 a unit, but Doc's rates plays from 1 to 8 units or more, so a few large winning plays can produce a big dollar total from an ordinary win rate. Our flat bet math above shows how far apart the two can be: The Quantitative Edge is 248-223, which is almost break even at flat stakes, yet it is advertised as +3,245.

The founding story does not hold one number. The homepage says 54 years, the house page says 55 years, the service page says almost 50 years and the roster page says the unit system was developed "over 38 years ago" and that the founder "has been the sole owner" since 1971. Gambling911 reported in December 2012 that Morris "Doc" Moseman had died and that his son had been heavily involved in running the service. None of this proves anything about the picks, but it shows how little the marketing copy is kept up to date.
record: Watchdog graded sample, new 22 Nov 2026. Doc's Sports does not publish a complete, time stamped log we can audit, so we built a sample from public posts that carry their plays. Watchdog captures X accounts and forum threads that post or repost picks; the ones naming Doc's Sports most often were vcsports, tgeorgecapper, IndianCowboyPix, BuzzKill (TheRX newsletters thread). From 24 Oct 2026 to 30 Oct 2026 we took every play our parser could read inside a Doc's Sports block, kept only those posted before the game started, removed repeats, and graded each one against the final score at one unit risked, at the odds shown or -110 when none were shown.
Result: 3 plays, 0 won, 3 lost, -3.00 units, a return of -100.0% per unit risked. By month: October 0 won, 3 lost, -3.00 units.
What it means: 3 decided plays is far too few to judge.

Doc's Sports does not publish a full, time stamped log of every pick with the line, the price and the post time, at least not on any page we could open without paying. The roster shows short runs and season totals chosen by the seller, and each handicapper's blurb is rewritten as runs change, so the set of numbers we saw on 20 Nov 2026 will not be the set a reader sees next month.

The only outside grading we came across was not a full record either. A Wayback Machine copy of the old OddsShark NFL computer picks page from 16 Jan 2025 carried boxes labelled "Sponsored Picks" from "Doc's Premium Picks", which means Doc's paid or partnered for that placement, not that anyone graded it. In 2021 a press release said Doc's had relaunched its text based Consensus Picks service "with new management" and claimed eight straight winning days and 43 units; today the same product is advertised as "23-8 +$3,500 Consensus run!". Neither figure comes with a log.

Posting times on the site do not agree. The FAQ says picks post "at 1 pm pacific on Fridays" with top college and NFL games on weekend mornings, while the current weekly football package says selections post Thursday at 6 p.m. Eastern. The FAQ appears out of date.

customers_intro: Independent buyer evidence on Doc's Sports is spread thin over almost twenty years: one Covers thread that started in 2008, two SBR threads from 2013 and 2017, a TheRX thread from 2025 and 2026, three Reddit posts and one PissedConsumer review. The testimonials on the Doc's site are chosen by Doc's. Below is everything we found and how much weight each piece can carry.

customers.text: We found about fifteen independent posts about Doc's Sports across Covers, Sportsbook Review, TheRX, Reddit and PissedConsumer, from 2008 to 2026. Most run against the service. The complaints repeat across sites and years: advertised runs that buyers say did not match what they received (Covers 2008, Covers 2016), a guarantee that only gives more picks (Covers 2016), losing free picks (SBR 2013), and forum regulars who say they bet against the biggest rated plays (SBR 2017, TheRX 2026). Two posters on SBR in 2017 alleged that Doc's earns from sportsbook affiliate deals and sends opposite sides to different buyers; neither showed proof. On the positive side, a buyer on SBR in 2017 said they had bought for years and found the picks consistent, a poster in 2018 reported a 10-2 stretch on one handicapper, a 2024 Reddit poster said a free trial put them up $2,300, and a 2026 PissedConsumer reviewer praised the handicappers and the live phone support. Nobody on either side posted a full log, and we could not verify any of these claims.

The Doc's service page says "handicapper reviews and customer comments" from members appear below and that more are added weekly. These are selected and published by the seller, so they cannot tell you what a typical buyer experiences.

PissedConsumer lists one rated review of DocSports, 5.0 stars. The reviewer praised the handicappers, naming Tony George, and the chance to reach a live person by phone, and said they had contacted the company before posting. One review is not a sample.

On TheRX, a member who said they track the Doc's handicappers daily wrote that they promote hot runs and "never mention their terrible cold streaks," named Doc's among the worst services of the 2026 season, and said they were up about 40 units betting against Doc's soccer and NBA picks before a hot week cut that roughly in half. They did not post a log, and we did not verify these figures.

The same TheRX thread was opened by a bettor who said they had used Doc's Sports off and on for more than 10 years and asked other customers for feedback. They did not post their results, and a later reply in August 2026 asked whether the critic above still had Doc's football picks.

A later TheRX reply agreed that honest profit and loss records are rare among pick sellers, said posting 10 to 15 picks a day is not serious, and warned against paying to join group buys. The post was about sellers in general, with Doc's as the thread's topic.
TheRX's daily service play thread rules list Doc's Sports and Doc Sports handicappers among the services whose plays may not be posted there. The rules do not give a reason.

An SBR member said they were thinking of buying a $3,000 a month package covering every 5.0 rated Doc's play, said they had bought Doc's subscriptions for years and found them very consistent, and later said they would track every bet. Other members accused the member of promoting the service, which they denied. They never posted their results in the thread.

In the same SBR thread one member wrote that Doc's was one of the biggest losing services and that betting against its 5 unit and bigger plays was profitable, and claimed a leaked sportsbook affiliate statement showed Doc's earning more than $25,000 from one book in one month. We found no document supporting this.

Another SBR member in that thread alleged that Doc's had emailed top rated picks on both sides of the same game, giving the 2017 college football title game as their example. They offered no screenshots, and we could not check it.

On the second page of the SBR thread a poster said they had followed one handicapper's plays a few days earlier and gone 10-2, and asked where to find that handicapper's official record. A reply told them to bet against the service instead.

A Covers thread was opened by a buyer who said Doc's advertised a 7-1 college run and a college Game of the Year that did not match their record, that they were down about 10 bets on the season, and that they were given another handicapper's picks to make up for it. Two other members said they had paid and would dispute the charge with their card company.

A Covers member said they had used Doc's twice, around 2005 and again in 2015, in college and pro football and basketball, never came out ahead, and that the service only offered more picks until losses were recovered. They said they suspected the posted claims were inflated.
A later reply in the same Covers thread said the service had long frustrated customers. The post also carried an unrelated link, so we give it little weight.
On SBR, a member said the Doc's free picks emailed to them had lost seven in a row. Free picks are a sample the seller chooses to give away, not the paid product.
A Covers member who opened a thread to rank the worst handicappers online placed Doc's Sports fifth, saying it had lots of bad picks. They gave no record.

On Reddit, a bettor who checks free picks sites said Doc's free MLB picks often took long shot sides and quoted odds that did not match the books they saw. Another user replied that they suspected the site was paid by sportsbooks to give poor picks, mostly underdogs, and called its MMA picks horrible. Neither offered evidence.

A Reddit poster wrote that a free trial with one Doc's handicapper had put them up $2,300 in about a week betting $100 a unit, and linked that handicapper's sales page. A post that links straight to a sales page may be promotion, so weigh it accordingly.

We did not find a Better Business Bureau profile we could confirm belongs to docsports.com, an app store listing, or any court or regulator record about the business. A Reddit post asking about docsports.com in August 2024 was removed by moderators with no replies.

conflicts: The Doc's FAQ says: "We suggest that you give a couple of these a try," about offshore sportsbooks it says it has confidence in, while adding that "Doc's does not endorse any illegal gambling activity." On 20 Nov 2026 its daily free pick listed the line as offered at BookMaker through a docsports.com tracking link. Sportsbook affiliate deals usually pay the referrer a share of what referred customers lose. That does not prove anything about the picks, but it is a financial interest a buyer should know about.
Offshore sportsbooks are not licensed by U.S. state regulators. Check the law where you live before you follow that advice.

Doc's picks are also sold through resellers. The Capperspicks profile lists Doc's packages behind Buy Now links to sportscapping.com carrying an affiliate code, at prices that differ from docsports.com. In January 2025 the OddsShark computer picks page showed "Sponsored Picks" boxes for "Doc's Premium Picks" beside its own free picks. Paid placement on other betting sites is marketing, not a record.
strengths: A long, documented history: a 2012 news obituary confirms the founder ran the service for more than 40 years.
A named operator, a mailing address, a toll free phone line with posted hours, and a buyer review that praised reaching a live person.
Prices and guarantee terms are written out per package, so a buyer can see the rules, including the profit thresholds, before paying.
The win percentages printed beside its records match their own win and loss counts in every case we tested.
Free picks, a weekly newsletter and a "Free $60 Account" offer let a reader see the style before buying, and a roster of named handicappers lets a buyer pick one sport specialist.
concerns: No full public record. Every number on the site is a run or total chosen by the seller, with no start dates, prices or unit sizes.
The same record is printed two different ways on one page in at least four places, and the business's age is given four different ways.
The roster page still says the founder has been the sole owner since 1971, years after a news report of his death.
The guarantee replaces a losing package with more picks or store credit. It never returns money, never covers betting losses, and season packages carry no guarantee at all.
The FAQ points readers to offshore sportsbooks, the free pick links to BookMaker, and the picks are also pushed through reseller affiliate links and sponsored boxes.
Independent buyer posts we found are mostly negative, and the few positive ones come without logs.
checklist: Ask Doc's for every pick from the last 12 months for the handicapper you are considering, with the line, the odds, the unit size and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units and dollars, not wins. Our math shows 248-223 at flat stakes is close to break even, even when it is advertised as +3,245.
Read the guarantee for your exact package. Day packages pay a credit, longer packages extend, and season packages carry no guarantee.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get at a licensed book where you live.
Do not follow the FAQ's advice about offshore sportsbooks without checking your local law.
faq: It is a real business, founded in 1971 by Morris "Doc" Moseman and still selling picks under a named operator with published prices and a phone line. We could not verify that its handicappers win over time, because it does not publish a full record of every pick, and the independent buyer posts we found are mostly negative.
What does the Watchdog sample of Doc's Sports show?
We graded 3 of their plays that were posted publicly before the game started, 24 Oct 2026 to 30 Oct 2026: 0 won, 3 lost, -3.00 units at one unit each. That is too few plays to judge.
How much does Doc's Sports cost?

On 20 Nov 2026 the house handicapper sold one day packages for $25 to $30, weekly packages for $89 to $99, monthly packages for $279 to $325, and season packages from $495 (rest of football season) to $850 (NBA). The 365 day soccer package was $795.

We found no cash refund terms. Losing weekly and monthly packages can be extended for free, losing one day packages get an account credit of about the package price, and the season packages show no guarantee.

The contact page names Doc's Enterprises of Sauk City, Wisconsin. The founder died in 2012 according to Gambling911, which said his son had been heavily involved in running the service, and a reseller profile names the son as the owner. The Doc's roster page still describes the founder as sole owner.
Are the Doc's Sports records verified?
No. The win percentages it prints match its own counts, but every record is a run or total chosen by the seller, with no full log, and some records appear with two different figures on the same page.
Not yet. No Doc's Sports handicapper is matched to a Watchdog graded record in this edition. If that changes, this page will say so and show the record.
